cards.title: Sperling: whole and partial report
cards.aim: How much does sensory (iconic) memory hold, and how long does it last?
cards.manipulated: The report method: whole report (name as many letters as you can), partial report (a tone cues one row right away), and delayed partial report (the tone comes after a delay). The displays were three rows of four letters.
cards.measured: How many letters people could report from a briefly flashed letter array.
cards.found: In whole report people named about a third of the letters. In partial report they named most of the cued row, for any row. In delayed partial report they named only about one letter, and by about one second partial report fell to near the whole-report level.
cards.means: Sensory memory has a large capacity but fast decay; the report limit came from the image fading, not from too little being stored.
cards.trap: Whole report makes capacity look like four or five items, but that is a limit on reporting, not on storage.

cards.title: Brown–Peterson: delay and trial history
cards.aim: How fast does short-term memory fade when rehearsal is blocked?
cards.manipulated: The delay before recall (a few seconds up to about eighteen seconds) and where a trial fell in the series (first trial, third trial, many trials later).
cards.measured: Recall of three letters after counting backward by threes during the delay.
cards.found: On the first trial recall stayed high even after the long delay. On later trials recall after the long delay dropped, and after many trials it fell to almost nothing. Averaged over all trials, recall fell with delay.
cards.means: Forgetting in short-term memory comes from proactive interference as well as decay; earlier trigrams made the new one harder to keep.
cards.trap: The average curve looks like pure decay over time, but it hides that the big drops came from later trials.

cards.title: Visual change detection and complexity
cards.aim: Is visual short-term memory capacity set by the number of items or by the amount of information in them?
cards.manipulated: Set size (number of colored squares), what changed in colored bars (angle, color, or both), and object complexity (colored squares, Chinese characters, random polygons, shaded cubes).
cards.measured: Whether people judged a second display (S2) the same as or different from a briefly flashed first display (S1).
cards.found: Accuracy fell dramatically above about four items. Remembering two features of a bar was about as easy as one. Capacity fell as objects got more complex, from about four for colored squares to fewer than two for shaded cubes.
cards.means: Visual short-term memory holds about three to four whole objects, and capacity depends on how much information each object carries.
cards.trap: Do not say the limit is always seven items; for visual memory the slides give about four, and fewer for complex objects.

cards.title: Digit-span training and chess expertise
cards.researcher: Ericsson and colleagues; Chase and Simon
cards.aim: Can chunking and knowledge let people hold much more in short-term memory?
cards.manipulated: For Ericsson: training a college student on digit span. For Chase and Simon: player skill (masters vs beginners) and board type (real-game arrangement vs random arrangement).
cards.measured: Digit span for the trained student; number of chess pieces placed correctly after a brief look at a board.
cards.found: The trained student's digit span rose to around eighty digits by chunking digits into running times. Masters placed far more pieces than beginners on real-game boards but were no better on random boards.
cards.means: Chunking with knowledge from long-term memory stretches capacity; experts do not have bigger short-term memories.
cards.trap: The masters' advantage disappears with random boards, so it is knowledge of real patterns, not a larger store.

cards.title: Conrad · sound-based errors after visual presentation
cards.aim: When letters are seen, are errors based on how they look or how they sound?
cards.manipulated: Whether the flashed letters were similar or not similar (half of the presentations each).
cards.measured: Writing down the letters after a brief visual flash.
cards.found: Errors more often swapped in a letter that sounded like the target (E replaced by B) than one that looked like it (F for E).
cards.means: Seen letters are recoded into a sound-based form in working memory (phonological similarity effect).
cards.trap: The letters came in through vision, but the confusions followed sound; presentation format is not the same as memory code.

cards.title: Word length, bilingual digit span, and articulatory suppression
cards.researcher: Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984); Ellis and Hennelly (1980)
cards.aim: What limits how much verbal material the phonological loop can hold?
cards.manipulated: Word length (short vs long words), language of the digits (Welsh vs English for bilingual children), and speaking while memorizing (articulatory suppression).
cards.measured: Memory for word lists and digit span.
cards.found: People remembered more short words than long words. Welsh-English bilingual children had a shorter digit span in Welsh because Welsh number names take longer to say. Suppression lowered recall and reduced both the word-length and phonological similarity effects.
cards.means: Verbal span depends on how much can be rehearsed in about 1.5 to 2 seconds, and speech-based rehearsal is used to maintain verbal information.
cards.trap: The Welsh-English gap comes from pronunciation time, not from the numbers' values.

cards.title: Brooks · sentence and F dual-task comparisons
cards.aim: Does a response interfere more when it uses the same kind of memory as the thing being held?
cards.manipulated: Response mode: speaking vs pointing, for two memory tasks (a memorized sentence with noun judgments, and a memorized F with inside/outside corner judgments).
cards.measured: How easy each task was under each response mode.
cards.found: With the sentence, pointing was easier than speaking. With the F, speaking was easier than pointing.
cards.means: Interference depends on the combination of tasks, which supports some independence between verbal and visual or spatial memory.
cards.trap: The results reverse across the two tasks, so neither speaking nor pointing is easier overall.

cards.title: Shepard and Metzler · angle and mental-rotation time
cards.aim: Do people mentally rotate objects, and does more rotation take more time?
cards.manipulated: The angle of rotation between pairs of block-built objects (picture-plane and depth rotation).
cards.measured: Reaction time to judge whether the two objects matched.
cards.found: For picture-plane pairs, reaction time increased as the angle increased, approximately linearly.
cards.means: Larger angles need a larger mental transformation, consistent with an active operation on a spatial representation.
cards.trap: Picture-plane rotation turns within the flat plane; depth rotation turns in three-dimensional space.

cards.title: Vogel · relevant load, distractors, and filtering efficiency
cards.aim: Do people with higher working-memory capacity keep irrelevant items out better?
cards.manipulated: Capacity group (higher vs lower) and display type: two relevant red bars, four relevant red bars, or two red bars plus two irrelevant blue bars.
cards.measured: A memory-related ERP response during the 900 ms retention interval, plus a change judgment on the relevant orientations.
cards.found: High-capacity people showed a larger response for four items than two, and little change when blue distractors were added. For low-capacity people, adding distractors raised the response toward the four-item level. Capacity correlated positively with filtering efficiency.
cards.means: Capacity depends on which items get in as well as how many targets there are; better filtering goes with higher capacity.
cards.trap: A bigger response means a stronger negative deflection, not a more positive voltage.

existing_explainers.title: Mental multiplication: 43 times 6
existing_explainers.plain: This shows storage and processing working together: you hold one number while you work on another.
steps: Hold the 8 in memory and carry the 1 over the 4.
6 x 4 = 24, then add the carried 1 to get 25.
Combine the 25 with the held 8 to get 258.
existing_explainers.example: Holding the 8 is storage; carrying the 1 and doing the next multiplication and addition is processing.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Do not say working memory only holds numbers; the 8 must survive while other operations are done.
explain: Working memory is a limited-capacity system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information during complex tasks such as comprehension, learning and reasoning. Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed it because the older picture of short-term memory was too simple: there, short-term memory was mostly a waiting room where information sat until it was used or lost. Storage keeps something on hand briefly, and manipulation works on it. The hard part to grasp is that both happen at the same moment and draw on one shared, limited capacity.

Multiplying 43 times 6 in your head is a small, concrete case of exactly that. You picture the whole problem and keep it in mind so later steps can return to it. You multiply 3 by 6 and get 18. You hold the 8 in memory as the ones digit and carry the 1 over to the 4. You multiply 6 by 4 to get 24 and add the carried 1 to make 25. Finally you combine that 25 with the 8 that has been held all along, and the answer is 258.

Keeping the 8 alive while everything else goes on is storage. Carrying, multiplying and adding are active processes, because each one changes the information. The common mistake is to treat working memory as a shelf that only holds things. The 8 has to last through several steps while other operations run, so the answer depends on storage and processing working together, and that combination is the job of working memory.

The same thing happens when you push a cart through a grocery store and keep a running bill in your head. Rice at 6 dollars and sauce at 4 give a total of 10, and that total is what you are holding. When the cheese at 5 goes in, you have to act on the held number, adding 5 and replacing it with 15. If you only kept the total, you would be staring at a number, and if you only added, you would have nothing to add to.

Because both jobs share one small amount of mental room, a friend calling out a question halfway down the aisle can make the total vanish. Capacity was spent on something else and the held number slipped away. In the same way, if the 8 slips away while you work on the tens, or the carried 1 is never added, the multiplication comes out wrong. Mental arithmetic is therefore a direct test of working memory: a kept piece and active work, done together, in the same limited workspace.

qa_facts.q: What is memory, and how did Endel Tulving describe episodic memory?
qa_facts.a: Memory includes retaining, retrieving and using information about stimuli, images, events, ideas and skills after the original information is no longer present. A past experience can influence current or future behavior without being visible in the environment. Endel Tulving described episodic memory as a kind of mental time travel, because remembering an event connects it back to the experienced past.

qa_facts.q: What are encoding, storage and retrieval, and why does a failure to remember not tell you which one went wrong?
qa_facts.a: Encoding converts information into a form that can be stored, storage keeps it, and retrieval brings it back out when it is needed. Memory is an active system that can organize and even alter information, so it is not a recording that is kept unchanged. Because a failure to use information could come from a problem at any of the three operations, forgetting on its own does not show which one failed. Forgetting a familiar name could mean it was never encoded well, was lost from storage, or cannot be retrieved right now.

qa_facts.q: How is the memory tree organized, and where do episodic and semantic memory sit in it?
qa_facts.a: The tree splits memory into sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory. Long-term memory then splits into declarative memory, which contains episodic events and semantic knowledge, and procedural memory, which concerns skills. Declarative memory therefore has two branches, episodic memory and semantic memory. So episodic and semantic memory are branches of declarative memory inside long-term memory. They are not extra short-term stores, and the classification sorts memories by function rather than claiming all memories last equally long or hold the same kind of content.

qa_facts.q: What are the three stores of Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) modal model, and what does each hold and for how long?
qa_facts.a: Sensory memory briefly retains incoming stimulation for seconds or fractions of a second. Short-term memory holds about five to seven items for roughly fifteen to twenty seconds. Long-term memory retains large amounts of information for years or even decades. Rehearsal is the control process that keeps information available in short-term memory and supports its transfer toward long-term memory.

qa_facts.q: What happens at each stage from looking at a phone directory to dialing a number?
qa_facts.a: Looking at the directory floods sensory memory with many pieces of visual information at once, and it is only held there very briefly. Attention picks out the one phone number you care about, and that selection moves it into short-term memory, while the rest of the directory is not carried forward. Repeating the number, which is maintenance rehearsal, keeps it available long enough to dial. If it is rehearsed enough it can become represented in long-term memory, so you no longer need the directory in view. Later you can retrieve it from long-term memory back into short-term memory to dial it, which shows that the flow goes both ways and is not only a one-way trip toward long-term storage.

qa_facts.q: What are an icon and an echo, and what does persistence of vision show about sensory memory?
qa_facts.a: An icon is the fleeting visual trace left by stimulation, and an echo is the brief continuation of auditory information after a sound ends. They differ in modality, vision versus hearing, and they are not the durable representations used to remember something much later. Persistence of vision is the brief retention of the perception of light, and it is why a sparkler seems to leave a trail and why film frames feel continuous. It shows that sensory memory holds a lot of information for a short interval, which fills the gaps between moments of input, but its large capacity does not mean long duration, because the information decays quickly.

qa_facts.q: What did Sperling (1960) do, and how do whole report, partial report and delayed partial report differ?
qa_facts.a: Sperling (1960) flashed an array of letters, three rows of four such as X M L T, A F N B, C D Z P, and asked what people had seen. The puzzle was whether people reported few letters because they only registered a few, or because the image faded before they could report everything. In whole report, participants report as many letters as they can. In partial report, a tone after the display tells them which row to report, so they cannot know in advance which row to memorize. In delayed partial report, the tone comes after an extra delay. The tone only comes after the display is gone, so strong partial report means information about all the rows was available at the start.

qa_facts.q: What were Sperling’s (1960) results, and what do they show about the capacity and duration of sensory memory?
qa_facts.a: In Sperling (1960), whole report averaged 4.5 of 12 letters, about 37.5 percent. Immediate partial report averaged 3.3 of 4 letters, about 82 percent, no matter which row was cued. Delayed partial report fell to about 1 of 4, or 25 percent, in the delayed-cue condition. Because people could report almost any cued row, far more than four or five letters must have been available at first, so the whole-report limit is a limit on reporting before the trace fades, not on what was perceived. Sensory memory therefore has a large capacity but fast decay, with most information lost within about one second unless it is selected for further processing. As the cue is delayed, partial-report accuracy drops toward the whole-report level, which links the advantage to a rapidly fading representation and does not support holding the whole array indefinitely.

qa_facts.q: What is memory span, and what is the traditional estimate for short-term memory?
qa_facts.a: Short-term memory holds small amounts briefly and is easily disrupted by interruption and interference. Memory span is the amount that can be recalled accurately in a task. The traditional estimate is seven plus or minus two units, but it depends on the kind of units and the task and should not be used for every visual-memory result.

qa_facts.q: How do recoding, maintenance rehearsal and elaborative rehearsal differ?
qa_facts.a: Recoding reorganizes or modifies information in short-term memory. Maintenance rehearsal repeats information to prolong its availability, like repeating a label. Elaborative rehearsal links new information with existing long-term knowledge, which supports longer-term learning. They are different control processes, because repeating a label is not the same as explaining how it relates to what you already know.

qa_facts.q: What does short-term memory do in current thought, what does Clive Wearing show, and how do duration and capacity differ?
qa_facts.a: Short-term memory includes selected sensory input and information retrieved from long-term memory, and it is what lets you understand a sentence, do arithmetic, dial a number or navigate. It acts as a window on the present, and this active availability differs from the large body of knowledge stored outside current awareness. Clive Wearing is a case of memory impairment. Keeping immediate information and remembering across events are different memory functions, so a case like his has to be analyzed function by function. Duration is how long information stays available and capacity is how much can be held. Rehearsal can extend duration and chunking can extend effective capacity, so a result can reflect the strategy used and not only the memory system.

qa_facts.q: Why did Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) have participants count backward by threes?
qa_facts.a: Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) presented three letters followed by a number, and participants counted backward by threes during a delay of 3 to 18 seconds and then recalled the letters. The counting prevents ordinary maintenance rehearsal, so participants cannot simply keep repeating the letters. Comparing the delays therefore measures retention when rehearsal is blocked.

qa_facts.q: What happened to recall after a long delay on the first trial versus many trials later in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
qa_facts.a: In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), on the first trial recall was high at three seconds and still relatively high at eighteen seconds, because no earlier letters from the task competed with the current set. By the third trial recall at eighteen seconds was lower than on the first trial, since earlier sets now competed. After many trials recall at long delays was substantially reduced, because accumulated earlier material interfered with the set being tested. The same delay did far more damage when more earlier material had piled up, so trial history matters and the drop is not only the passage of eighteen seconds.

qa_facts.q: Why does the average over all trials give a misleading impression in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
qa_facts.a: In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), the average over all trials makes it look like a steady loss with time, as though short-term memory simply decays. But the average mixes very different trials together. Early trials have high recall even at 18 seconds, and later trials have very low recall at 18 seconds. The steep drop comes mostly from the later trials, where proactive interference is strongest, so averaging hides interference behind something that looks like decay. Decay is loss associated with the passage of time, and proactive interference is when earlier information disrupts remembering newer information. Because earlier trials affect later recall, the Brown–Peterson pattern is evidence for interference and challenges treating every loss as pure time-based decay. The effective duration is about 15 to 20 seconds, and rehearsal and interference conditions affect the outcome.

qa_facts.q: Which concept describes earlier trigrams making new letters harder to recall in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959)?
qa_facts.a: It is proactive interference, which occurs when earlier information disrupts remembering newer information. In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), earlier trials affect later recall, because the trigrams from earlier trials compete with the one being tested, so the loss is not explained solely by elapsed time.

qa_facts.q: How does retroactive interference differ from proactive interference, and what is an example of each?
qa_facts.a: The direction of the competition is what differs. Retroactive interference is when new information disrupts memory for older information, so the affected memory is the old one and the interfering information arrived later. Learning a new phone number making the old number harder to retrieve is the example. Proactive interference is when old information disrupts memory for newer information, such as previous parking locations interfering with remembering where you parked today. Routine events are especially vulnerable because similar memories compete, and both types can be reduced when events are distinctive. To label it correctly, first decide which information is being recalled, then ask whether the competitor came earlier or later.

qa_facts.q: What is digit span, and how is it scored?
qa_facts.a: Digit span is the longest sequence of digits recalled correctly in order. The lists get longer, from four items to ten, and the longest list reproduced completely and in order defines the span. Getting the digits right but out of order does not count, one successful short list does not establish the limit, and one missed digit makes a longer list incorrect. Capacity differs between individuals and can be affected by strategies.

qa_facts.q: What did Miller (1956) propose, and how do Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) change the picture?
qa_facts.a: Miller (1956), in The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two, proposed that short-term capacity is about seven units, where the unit can differ across tasks, such as digits, words, numbers or phrases. The title is not proof that every short-term system holds exactly seven raw sensory elements. A unit can hold different amounts of information, so Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) compared colored squares with more complex objects using change detection. Their alternative emphasis is on the amount or complexity of information, not a fixed number of equally sized items.

qa_facts.q: How does the change-detection task of Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) work, and what did it show about visual short-term memory capacity?
qa_facts.a: Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) used change detection to measure visual short-term memory, VSTM, by comparing displays after a delay. Participants briefly view a first array, S1, for 100 milliseconds, and it then disappears, so they must keep the relevant visual properties in memory. A second display, S2, appears for 2,000 milliseconds and they judge whether it is the same or different. Correct answers require comparing S2 with the remembered S1, not looking at two arrays at once. Accuracy falls sharply when the set size goes above roughly four items, giving a capacity of about three to four items in visual working memory. That differs from the seven-plus-or-minus-two estimate for other tasks, and different tasks do not have to measure one identical capacity.

qa_facts.q: How does stimulus complexity affect visual capacity in Alvarez and Cavanagh’s (2004) work?
qa_facts.a: In Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004), same–different performance depends on how complex the stimuli are. Colored squares support a higher estimated capacity than more complex polygons or shaded cubes, and Chinese-character-like forms were also compared. Treating every stimulus as an equally sized item hides these differences, because capacity is constrained by the amount of information needed to represent the objects. Familiarity and the structure given to a stimulus can also change what counts as a unit of information. So a capacity for one category of stimulus is not a universal estimate for all visual objects.

qa_facts.q: What is chunking, and what did Ericsson and colleagues (1980) show?
qa_facts.a: Chunking combines smaller units into larger meaningful units. Ericsson and colleagues (1980) trained a student to reach a digit span of 79 by using familiar running times to organize the digits. The gain depends on knowledge-based organization, not on expanding every raw memory limit equally.

qa_facts.q: What did Chase and Simon (1973) find about chess recall, and what do control processes lead to?
qa_facts.a: In Chase and Simon (1973), chess masters recall more correct piece placements than beginners for meaningful game positions, but the advantage is greatly reduced for random arrangements. The experts’ edge comes from chunks that represent familiar relationships among pieces, and randomizing those relationships removes most of the benefit even though the pieces are the same kinds. Control processes include rehearsal, strategies for making material memorable such as the memory palace, and directing attention, and considering these active operations leads toward working memory, which concerns using and managing currently available information.

qa_facts.q: What is working memory according to Baddeley and Hitch (1974), and why does mental multiplication of 43 × 6 need both storage and processing?
qa_facts.a: Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed working memory as a limited-capacity system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information. Storage keeps information available for immediate use, and manipulation changes or works with it while it stays available. It is needed because treating short-term memory as passive storage is too simple, since comprehension, learning and reasoning require holding and operating on information together. In 43 × 6, first 3 × 6 = 18, the 8 is held as the ones digit (storage) and the 1 is carried over the 4 (an operation). Then 6 × 4 = 24, plus the carried 1 gives 25, and combining it with the held 8 gives 258. The 8 has to survive while another multiplication and an addition are carried out, which is exactly keeping a result available while changing other parts of the problem.

qa_facts.q: How does Baddeley and Hitch’s (1974) working-memory model differ from Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) short-term memory?
qa_facts.a: In Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) model, a single short-term component holds different types of information for a short time, and the emphasis is on temporary availability. Baddeley and Hitch’s (1974) model separates the system into the central executive, the visuospatial sketchpad and the phonological loop, so visual and spatial information can be maintained in a different component from verbal and auditory information, with the central executive coordinating their use. Working memory is used for manipulating information during complex cognition. The episodic buffer is a fourth component added by Baddeley in 2000, so it belongs to the expanded model and not the original three-component proposal.

qa_facts.q: What are the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and the central executive, and how do they connect to long-term knowledge?
qa_facts.a: The phonological loop maintains verbal and auditory information, with a phonological store that holds it and an articulatory rehearsal process that keeps it active by repeating the sounds, even silently. The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual information, what something looks like, and spatial information, where its parts are and how they are arranged. The central executive pulls information from long-term memory, coordinates the other components, and directs and maintains attention, and it is not a store for a particular kind of information. All the components interact with long-term knowledge, so a calculation can use verbal rehearsal of a result together with a visual picture of the digits.

qa_facts.q: What are the phonological similarity effect, the word-length effect and articulatory suppression, and what does each one tell you about the phonological loop?
qa_facts.a: The phonological similarity effect is confusion between letters or words that sound alike, even when they look different. The word-length effect is that memory for lists is better for short words than long words, because longer words take more time to rehearse and produce. Articulatory suppression is speaking while trying to remember other material, which occupies the rehearsal process and so reduces memory. Similarity is about confusion between sound patterns, word length is about the time needed to repeat the items, and suppression is about interfering with rehearsal itself. Together they show that verbal maintenance depends on sound-based codes and speech-related rehearsal.

qa_facts.q: What did Conrad (1964) find, and why does it show that visually presented letters are remembered by sound?
qa_facts.a: Conrad (1964) briefly flashed letters, half the time similar and half not, and asked participants to write them down. Errors were more likely to swap in a letter that sounded like the target than one that only looked like it. An E was likely to be replaced by a B, which sounds similar, while a visually similar substitution such as F for E was less likely. The letters came in through vision, but the confusions followed their spoken names. So remembering a seen letter can involve converting it into a sound-based representation through the phonological loop. The key distinction is between the presentation format, what people see, and the memory code, the form in which it is maintained.

qa_facts.q: What did Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984) find about word length?
qa_facts.a: Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984) found that people remembered more short words than long words. The word-length effect concerns how long the items take to pronounce and rehearse, so a list of longer words takes more time to repeat and fewer words can be refreshed within the same brief rehearsal period.

qa_facts.q: What did Ellis and Hennelly (1980) find about digit span in Welsh and English?
qa_facts.a: Ellis and Hennelly (1980) found that Welsh–English bilingual children had a shorter digit span in Welsh than in English. The children knew both languages, but Welsh number names take longer to pronounce, so the difference follows the time needed to say the number names and not the numbers themselves. Span is related to the amount of verbal material that can be said in about 1.5 to 2 seconds, so faster rehearsal lets more items be kept active.

qa_facts.q: What happens to memory, the word-length effect and the phonological similarity effect under articulatory suppression, and why?
qa_facts.a: When a person speaks while memorizing, the competing speech keeps the phonological loop busy, so there is less opportunity to rehearse and recall gets worse. The word-length effect is reduced, because short words normally win by being quicker to rehearse, and when rehearsal is occupied neither list gets ordinary rehearsal. The phonological similarity effect is also reduced, because the conversion of seen items into sounds is disrupted, so sound overlap has less influence. This connects the memory effects to a particular process, speech-related rehearsal used to maintain verbal information.

qa_facts.q: What did Brooks (1968) find in the sentence task?
qa_facts.a: The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information, such as the shape of an object and where its parts are. In Brooks (1968), participants memorized a sentence and decided for each word whether it was a noun, responding either by speaking or by pointing. Pointing was easier, because maintaining and processing the sentence occupied the phonological loop, and speaking the answers also required verbal processing and competed with it.

qa_facts.q: What did Brooks (1968) find in the F task, and what does the opposite pattern show?
qa_facts.a: In Brooks (1968), participants memorized the shape of an F, mentally followed its outline and classified each corner as an inside or an outside corner, responding either by speaking or by pointing to response locations. Speaking was easier, because holding and following the F used the visuospatial sketchpad, and pointing to spatially arranged responses added a competing spatial demand. This is the opposite of the sentence-task result, and it shows that verbal and visual–spatial memory are at least partly independent. A task is easier when the information held and the operation performed use different types of short-term memory.

qa_facts.q: What did Shepard and Metzler (1971) find about mental rotation, and what does the pattern of reaction times mean?
qa_facts.a: Shepard and Metzler (1971) presented pairs of block-built objects at different orientations, and participants judged whether the objects matched. Mental rotation means turning a representation in mind to compare how its parts line up, and the rotation can be in the picture plane or in depth. For picture-plane pairs, reaction time increased as the angle of rotation increased, approximately linearly, so small angles were answered faster than large ones. A larger angle requires a larger mental transformation before the objects can be compared. This suggests an active operation on a spatial representation, not just storage of an unchanged picture.

qa_facts.q: What does the central executive do, what are updating, shifting and inhibition, and why is the executive called a homunculus?
qa_facts.a: The central executive does the work of working memory by directing and maintaining attention, which includes focusing on relevant information, dividing attention across demands and switching attention when the task changes. It also suppresses irrelevant information, coordinates the sketchpad and the phonological loop, and performs calculations. Miyake and colleagues (2000) distinguish updating, which changes the information currently maintained, shifting, which changes the task or operation being performed, and inhibition, which suppresses information or responses that interfere with the goal. The executive is criticized as a homunculus, a little internal agent given the job of controlling everything, because naming a controller does not explain how control is done. Splitting it into updating, shifting and inhibition specifies different operations inside what would otherwise be one broad label.

qa_facts.q: What is the episodic buffer, and what evidence supports a component that goes beyond the loop and the sketchpad?
qa_facts.a: Baddeley (2000) added the episodic buffer as a fourth component. It has a limited capacity of about four chunks, and it binds information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. Binding means keeping different kinds of information together as a connected representation. People can immediately recall about 16 words from a meaningful sentence, more than their span for unrelated words, because meaning and long-term language knowledge let the words be kept as connected material. Some amnesic patients can immediately recall a just-heard story, so immediate retention of an organized episode can be present even when longer-term memory is impaired.

qa_facts.q: What did Vogel and colleagues (2005) do in their working-memory task?
qa_facts.a: Vogel and colleagues (2005) first measured working-memory capacity to separate higher- and lower-capacity participants. Participants then did a visual memory task while event-related potentials (ERPs), electrical brain responses, were recorded. A cue pointed to one side of the display, red bars were shown for 100 milliseconds, there was a 900 millisecond retention interval, and then a test display where they judged whether a relevant orientation had changed. The more complex displays also had irrelevant blue bars, so ignoring them required selection within the display.

qa_facts.q: What did Vogel and colleagues (2005) find about capacity and filtering efficiency?
qa_facts.a: In Vogel and colleagues (2005), the memory-related response continues into the retention interval, and for high-capacity participants it is greater with four relevant items than with two. Adding two blue distractors to two red targets changed little for high-capacity participants, so they kept the irrelevant items out. For low-capacity participants, the distractors raised the response toward the four-item level, meaning irrelevant material entered working memory. Capacity was positively correlated with filtering efficiency, so people with higher capacity are also less distracted, and a lower score can reflect competing material occupying processing that targets needed.
